::: {.lead}
Rami must test *Pocket Quest 1.2* on P5 (Android) and on P8 (an iPhone).
In lecture 13 you saw that the two systems are built differently. Today you
see the difference in your hands: where each phone shows its version, how
a test build reaches each phone, how each one asks for permissions, and
what each one does to a game when the battery is low. In this seminar you
explore these features on your own phone and compare them with a phone of
the other system. Every section ends with a task, and at the end you can
write a short comparison of the two phones.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary api-level security-patch developer-options usb-debugging beta-build runtime-permission power-saving-mode focus-mode >}}

## 14.1 Versions and test builds

A bug report always names the phone and the **OS version**: a bug may
appear on Android 13 but not on Android 15. And before a test, the test
build must reach the phone. Each system does both in its own way
(@fig-ver).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 14.1 — Version, patch and test builds"}
- **Android:** Settings › About phone shows the Android version, the
  **security patch** date and the build number. Each version has an **API
  level**, the number that a game uses to say the oldest Android it
  supports. Tapping the build number 7 times shows **developer options**;
  there, **USB debugging** lets a PC install a test build (`.apk`) and read
  the log.
- **iPhone:** Settings › General › About shows the iOS version. A test
  build (a **beta build**) comes through Apple's TestFlight app, or from a
  Mac with Xcode. Apple updates all supported iPhones at the same time.
:::

![Where the two phones show their version, and how a test build reaches them. Example values.](images/versions-builds.png){#fig-ver width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 14.1 — Installing the build on P5"}
1. Rami opens Settings › About phone on P5 and taps Build number 7 times:
   "You are now a developer".
2. In Settings › System › Developer options he turns on USB debugging.
3. He connects P5 to the PC and allows the PC once. The PC installs
   `PocketQuest_1.2_android.apk`.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 14.2 — The build on P8"}
1. Byte Bay uploads the iOS build to TestFlight and invites Rami.
2. Rami installs TestFlight from the App Store on P8, and then Pocket Quest
   1.2 from TestFlight.
3. He writes P8's model and iOS version in the report.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Leaving USB debugging on after the test, or installing `.apk` files from
unknown websites. Both open the phone to harm. Turn developer options off
on a personal phone, and install builds only from your studio.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Read your version"}
1. Find the OS version of your phone (and, on Android, the security patch
   date).
2. Ask a classmate with a phone of the other system for the same lines.
   Which phone got its last update later?

*Your result:* two versions and one sentence.
:::

## 14.2 Permissions and privacy

The new version of Pocket Quest has a map of real places and a voice chat.
It asks for the location and the microphone. Both systems ask the user
while the app runs: a **runtime permission** (@fig-perm, lecture 13).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 14.2 — Runtime permission"}
A **runtime permission** is asked the first time an app needs the camera,
the microphone, the location, the contacts or notifications. For the
location, both systems offer: while using the app; only this time (iPhone:
Allow Once); or do not allow. The user can change every permission later
(Android: Settings › Apps › the app › Permissions; iPhone: Settings › the
app).
:::

![The location question on Android and on iPhone.](images/permission-dialog.png){#fig-perm width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 14.3 — Rami answers three questions"}
1. Location for the map, in a one-day test: **Only this time** on P5,
   **Allow Once** on P8.
2. Microphone: the test has no voice chat, so **Don't allow**.
3. Notifications: the test checks the daily reward message, so **Allow**.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Allowing everything to "make the game work". An app should get only what it
needs; a game that asks for the contacts without a reason is a warning
sign.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Check the permissions"}
1. Open the permission page of one game and one other app on your phone.
2. Turn off one permission that the app does not need. Does the app still
   work?

*Your result:* the permissions of two apps and one change.
:::

## 14.3 Power saving, Do not disturb and the game

A test must show the game as players see it. But phones change how games
run when the battery is low, and notifications can cover the game
(@fig-power).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 14.3 — Power-saving mode and Do not disturb"}
The **power-saving mode** (Android: Battery saver; iPhone: Low Power Mode)
makes the battery last longer: it lowers the CPU speed and often the frame
rate and the brightness, and stops background work. Many phones offer it
at about 20 %. **Do not disturb** (on iPhone one of the Focus modes)
silences calls and notifications for a time.
:::

![Normal mode and power-saving mode during a game. Round example numbers.](images/power-modes.png){#fig-power width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 14.4 — P8 at 18 %"}
1. P8 shows "Low Power Mode?" at 18 %. If Rami says yes, Pocket Quest may
   drop from 60 to about 30 fps.
2. The report would show a slow game that players with a charged phone do
   not see.
3. Rami says no, charges P8 above 50 %, and turns on Do Not Disturb in
   the Control Centre.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/power-lab.html" poster="sims/power-lab.png" title="Power Lab: battery saver, Do not disturb and a game" height="620" >}}

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Testing with the power-saving mode on, to "save the battery". The test then
measures the power-saving mode, not the game. Charge the phone instead
(lecture 12).
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Find the switches"}
1. Find the power-saving mode and Do not disturb on your phone (Android:
   quick settings; iPhone: Control Centre).
2. In **Power Lab**, set the battery to 20 % and turn power saving on. What
   happens to the frame rate and the play time?

*Your result:* where the two switches are, and two numbers from the lab.
:::

## Case study: Two Phones

Rami prepares the test of *Pocket Quest 1.2* on P5 (Android) and P8 (an
iPhone). He needs the Android version and the security patch of P5, and he
installs the test build on both phones. Pocket Quest asks P8 for the
microphone, and P5 for the location for one test. Notifications must not
appear during the test, and at 18 % P8 asks to turn on Low Power Mode. The
Game challenge of the interactive lesson uses this story. In the mini-game
below you choose each step.

## Further reading

Android Help, "Find and change your Android version" and "Change app
permissions on your Android phone"; Apple Support, "Use Low Power Mode to
save battery life on your iPhone" and "Control access to information in
apps on iPhone"; Apple Developer, "TestFlight".

## Exercises

1. Where does an Android phone show its version and security patch?
2. Where does an iPhone show its iOS version?
3. How do you show developer options on Android?
4. What does USB debugging let a PC do?
5. How does a beta build of a game reach an iPhone?
6. Which location answer gives the location only now, on Android and on
   iPhone?
7. A puzzle game asks for the contacts. What do you answer, and why?
8. What does the power-saving mode do to a game?
9. Why should a tester not use the power-saving mode during a test?
10. Where do you turn on Do not disturb on an iPhone?

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. Settings › About phone.
2. Settings › General › About.
3. Tap Build number 7 times in About phone.
4. Install a test build and read the phone's log.
5. Through TestFlight (or a Mac with Xcode).
6. Android: Only this time. iPhone: Allow Once.
7. Don't allow: a puzzle game does not need the contacts.
8. It lowers the CPU speed and often the frame rate and the brightness.
9. The test would show a slower game than players see.
10. In the Control Centre (a Focus: Do Not Disturb).
:::
